questions.stem: A 47 year old woman has a 5 year history of a daily cough productive of large amounts of green sputum, sometimes flecked with blood. She had measles pneumonia as a child. She has never smoked. Her temperature is 36.8°C, pulse rate 78 bpm, BP 122/76 mmHg, respiratory rate 16 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 96% breathing air. There are coarse crackles at both bases.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Chronic copious purulent sputum with red specks and coarse crackles after childhood pneumonia is classic bronchiectasis; COPD is unlikely in a never smoker.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

clues: large amounts of green sputum, sometimes flecked with blood
steps.x: Years of copious purulent sputum with red specks after a childhood infection = permanently dilated bronchi.

elim: Gives variable wheeze, not years of copious purulent sputum with blood after childhood pneumonia.
She has never smoked, and daily copious purulent sputum after childhood pneumonia points to dilated airways.
Gives a dry cough with fine velcro crackles, not copious green sputum.
Would give fever, night sweats and weight loss; her sputum story and childhood infection fit bronchiectasis.

steps.x: B: Bronchiectasis. Previous infection is the most important cause of bronchiectasis.

questions.stem: A 71 year old man has had a cough productive of purulent sputum most days for 6 years. He was treated for pulmonary tuberculosis in his forties. He has no other illnesses and has normal bowel habit. HRCT shows dilated, thick-walled bronchi in both upper lobes. His immunoglobulins are normal.
questions.q: Which is the most likely cause of his bronchiectasis?
questions.e: Post-infective bronchiectasis is the commonest type; previous TB classically damages the upper lobes. Immunodeficiency is excluded by normal immunoglobulins.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most likely cause of his bronchiectasis?

clues: treated for pulmonary tuberculosis in his forties
steps.x: Symptoms started after TB, with upper lobe damage and normal immunity.

elim: Occurs in asthma with eosinophilia and raised IgE; he has no asthma.
Presents in childhood or young adults with pancreatic dysfunction; he is 71 with normal bowels.
Starts in early childhood with sinusitis and infertility, not after TB in middle age.
No joint disease is described.

steps.x: C: Previous pulmonary tuberculosis. Previous infection (pneumonia or TB) is the most important cause.

questions.stem: A 34 year old woman with long-standing asthma has had worsening wheeze and coughing up brown plugs of mucus for 3 months. Her temperature is 37.2°C, pulse rate 84 bpm, BP 118/72 mmHg, respiratory rate 18 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 96% breathing air. HRCT shows central (proximal) bronchiectasis.
questions.q: Which is the most likely cause of her bronchiectasis?
questions.e: ABPA occurs in asthmatics and gives brown mucus plugs and proximal bronchiectasis; it is treated with corticosteroids.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most likely cause of her bronchiectasis?
Asthma + brown mucus plugs + central bronchiectasis = hypersensitivity to Aspergillus.

elim: Would show from childhood with pancreatic disease; brown mucus plugs in an asthmatic suggest Aspergillus.
Gives recurrent bacterial infections, not asthma with brown plugs and eosinophilic features.
No history of pneumonia; asthma with brown plugs and central bronchiectasis is the clue.
Lifelong wet cough and sinusitis from early childhood, not asthma with mucus plugs.

steps.x: A: Allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis. ABPA is a cause of bronchiectasis and is treated with corticosteroids.

questions.stem: A 29 year old man has had five chest infections in two years, two needing hospital admission, plus recurrent sinusitis. He now coughs up purulent sputum every day and HRCT shows bilateral lower lobe bronchiectasis. He does not have diarrhoea or infertility. Blood tests are sent.
questions.q: Which is the most likely underlying cause?
questions.e: Low IgG, IgA and IgM with recurrent sinopulmonary infection point to antibody deficiency (e.g. CVID), an immunodeficiency cause of bronchiectasis.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most likely underlying cause?

clues: five chest infections in two years
steps.x: Recurrent bacterial sinopulmonary infections with low IgG, IgA and IgM.

elim: Needs asthma and raised IgE; all his immunoglobulins are low.
Immunoglobulins are normal or high in CF; his are all low.
Causes sinusitis and bronchiectasis but immunoglobulins are normal.
No joint symptoms, and RA does not lower all immunoglobulin classes.

steps.x: C: Primary antibody deficiency. Check immunoglobulins in new bronchiectasis: immunodeficiency is a treatable cause.

questions.stem: A 64 year old woman has had rheumatoid arthritis for 15 years, treated with sulfasalazine. Over the last 2 years she has developed a daily cough productive of purulent sputum and two chest infections. She has ulnar deviation of both hands. She has coarse crackles at the right base. HRCT shows dilated bronchi larger than their accompanying arteries.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: RA is a recognised cause of bronchiectasis; bronchi larger than the adjacent artery is the signet ring sign. RA-ILD gives a dry cough with fine crackles instead.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

clues: dilated bronchi larger than their accompanying arteries
steps.x: RA plus productive cough and dilated bronchi on HRCT.

elim: She takes sulfasalazine, not methotrexate, and has a productive not dry cough.
Nodules are usually silent; HRCT shows dilated bronchi, not nodules.
Gives dry cough, fine crackles and reticulation, not purulent sputum and dilated bronchi.
No dry eyes or mouth are described; the HRCT finding is bronchial dilation.

steps.x: C: Rheumatoid arthritis-associated bronchiectasis. Rheumatoid arthritis is a recognised cause of bronchiectasis.

questions.stem: A 58 year old man has had bronchiectasis for 20 years after whooping cough as a child. He coughs up a large volume of purulent sputum every day. His temperature is 36.9°C, pulse rate 82 bpm, BP 130/80 mmHg, respiratory rate 18 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 94% breathing air. He has coarse inspiratory crackles at both bases.
questions.q: Which is the most likely finding on examination of his hands?
questions.e: Clubbing is a sign of advanced bronchiectasis (chronic suppurative lung disease); the other signs point to liver, iron or cardiac problems.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most likely finding on examination of his hands?

clues: large volume of purulent sputum every day
steps.x: Long-standing, advanced suppurative lung disease.

elim: Linked to alcohol and liver disease, not suppurative lung disease.
A sign of iron deficiency, not chronic lung sepsis.
Suggests liver disease or pregnancy.
Point to infective endocarditis or trauma.

steps.x: B: Finger clubbing. Advanced bronchiectasis causes finger clubbing.

questions.stem: A 55 year old woman has bronchiectasis confirmed on HRCT after years of a daily productive cough. She has never smoked and has no history of asthma. Her oxygen saturation is 96% breathing air. She has coarse crackles and scattered wheeze. She has spirometry to assess her disease (see item resources).

visual.title: FEV1/FVC ratio
visual.label: Her ratio 0.58
visual.caption: A ratio below 0.7 means airflow obstruction.

questions.q: Which is the most likely spirometry result?
questions.e: Bronchiectasis gives an obstructive pattern (FEV1/FVC below 0.7); a preserved or raised ratio with low FVC would be restrictive.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most likely spirometry result?
Bronchiectasis is an airway disease: expect obstruction.

elim: Both reduced with a preserved ratio is restrictive, as in fibrosis.
Normal spirometry; her wheeze and disease suggest airflow obstruction.
A raised ratio with low FVC is restrictive, not obstructive.
Normal values; bronchiectasis typically gives obstruction.

steps.x: A: FEV1 62% predicted, FVC 88% predicted, FEV1/FVC 0.58. Spirometry in bronchiectasis shows an obstructive pattern, FEV1/FVC below 0.7.

questions.stem: A 21 year old woman has had a productive cough and chest infections since childhood. She now has haemoptysis. She was diagnosed with diabetes at 17 and takes pancreatic enzyme capsules with meals. She is underweight. She has finger clubbing and coarse crackles over both lungs. HRCT shows widespread bronchiectasis.
questions.q: Which is the most likely underlying cause?
questions.e: CF-related bronchiectasis: a young patient with productive cough, haemoptysis, clubbing and both exocrine (enzymes) and endocrine (diabetes) pancreatic failure.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most likely underlying cause?
Young patient, bronchiectasis, plus exocrine and endocrine pancreatic failure.

elim: Causes basal emphysema and liver disease, not pancreatic insufficiency with diabetes.
Causes malabsorption but not bronchiectasis or pancreatic enzyme need.
Causes recurrent infections but not exocrine and endocrine pancreatic failure.
Causes bronchiectasis and sinusitis but the pancreas is normal.

steps.x: C: Cystic fibrosis. Bronchiectasis plus pancreatic dysfunction in a young person = cystic fibrosis.

questions.stem: A 9 year old boy has had a wet cough every day since infancy and constant nasal discharge. He has bilateral glue ear. His heart sounds are loudest to the right of the sternum. His temperature is 36.7°C and oxygen saturation 96% breathing air. A chest X-ray shows the cardiac apex on the right. HRCT shows bronchiectasis in both lower lobes.
questions.q: Which is the most likely underlying cause?
questions.e: Dextrocardia, chronic rhinosinusitis, glue ear and bronchiectasis are Kartagener syndrome, a form of primary ciliary dyskinesia.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most likely underlying cause?

clues: wet cough every day since infancy
steps.x: Bronchiectasis + chronic upper airway disease + dextrocardia (Kartagener).

elim: Can cause bronchiectasis and sinus disease but not a right-sided heart.
Gives localised disease on one side, not bilateral disease with dextrocardia.
Causes infections but not situs inversus.
No history of whooping cough; dextrocardia points to a ciliary defect.

steps.x: E: Primary ciliary dyskinesia. Primary ciliary dyskinesia is a cause of bronchiectasis; with situs inversus it is Kartagener syndrome.

questions.stem: A 50 year old man is seen in a respiratory clinic. He has a daily cough producing about half a cup of foul purulent sputum. He has never smoked. HRCT shows bronchi that are wider than their neighbouring arteries and do not taper towards the periphery. He asks what the condition is.
questions.q: Which best describes the abnormality underlying his condition?
o: Destruction of alveolar walls distal to the terminal bronchiole
Mucous gland hypertrophy with normal bronchial calibre
Permanent dilation of the bronchi with impaired mucus clearance
questions.e: Bronchiectasis is permanent, irreversible bronchial dilation with impaired mucus clearance and recurrent infection; mucous gland hypertrophy alone is chronic bronchitis.

steps.x: The question asks: Which best describes the abnormality underlying his condition?

clues: do not taper towards the periphery
steps.x: Non-tapering bronchi wider than the artery = dilated bronchi.

elim: That is emphysema; his bronchi themselves are dilated.
Interstitial fibrosis gives honeycombing and a dry cough.
That is chronic bronchitis; his HRCT shows dilated bronchi.
That is asthma; bronchiectasis is irreversible dilation.

steps.x: D: Permanent dilation of the bronchi with impaired mucus clearance. Bronchiectasis is permanent bronchial dilation causing poor mucus clearance and recurrent infection.

questions.stem: A 68 year old woman with post-infective bronchiectasis has 5 days of increased cough and thicker, greener sputum than usual. She has never had a positive sputum culture. Her temperature is 37.6°C, pulse rate 92 bpm, BP 134/80 mmHg, respiratory rate 19 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 95% breathing air. A sputum sample is sent.
questions.q: Which organism is most likely to be grown?
questions.e: H. influenzae is the commonest exacerbation organism in bronchiectasis; Pseudomonas also colonises damaged airways.

steps.x: The question asks: Which organism is most likely to be grown?

clues: never had a positive sputum culture
steps.x: A routine exacerbation with no previous growth.

elim: Causes ABPA in asthmatics, not the usual bacterial exacerbation.
Causes atypical pneumonia with hyponatraemia, not bronchiectasis exacerbations.
Causes atypical pneumonia in young adults.
Seen more in CF and after influenza; not the commonest here.

steps.x: B: Haemophilus influenzae. Haemophilus influenzae is the most common organism in bronchiectasis exacerbations.

questions.stem: A 62 year old man has bronchiectasis. Over 3 days his sputum has increased in volume and become more purulent, and he is more breathless. His temperature is 37.8°C, pulse rate 96 bpm, BP 128/78 mmHg, respiratory rate 20 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 94% breathing air. Chest X-ray is unchanged from last year.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Increased sputum volume and purulence with breathlessness and no new consolidation is an infective exacerbation; pneumonia would show new shadowing.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

clues: increased in volume and become more purulent
Chest X-ray is unchanged from last year
steps.x: More sputum, more purulent, more breathless, no new X-ray change.

elim: Gives frothy pink sputum, orthopnoea and bilateral crackles with X-ray changes, not purulent sputum.
Would show new consolidation on the chest X-ray.
Would show a cavity with an air-fluid level; his X-ray is unchanged.
Pleuritic pain and tachycardia without increased purulent sputum; X-ray often normal but the sputum change points to infection.

steps.x: B: Infective exacerbation of bronchiectasis. An exacerbation = worse cough, sputum volume or purulence; recurrent exacerbations drive progressive lung damage.

questions.stem: A 66 year old woman has had bronchiectasis for 25 years. Over the last 5 years she has had four or five infective exacerbations each year and her FEV1 has fallen from 2.1 L to 1.4 L. She takes her physiotherapy irregularly. Her oxygen saturation is 93% breathing air.
questions.q: Which is the most likely cause of the decline in her lung function?
o: Development of emphysema from passive smoking
Recurrent infective exacerbations causing progressive airway damage
questions.e: Recurrent exacerbations drive progressive lung damage through the vicious cycle of infection, inflammation and impaired clearance; normal ageing cannot explain a 700 mL fall.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most likely cause of the decline in her lung function?

clues: four or five infective exacerbations each year
steps.x: Frequent exacerbations and poor airway clearance with falling FEV1.

elim: No smoke exposure is given, and the decline tracks her exacerbations.
Would cause stridor and a flattened flow-volume loop, not a link with infections.
Ageing loses about 30 mL a year, far less than 700 mL in 5 years.
Bronchial dilation in bronchiectasis is permanent.

steps.x: D: Recurrent infective exacerbations causing progressive airway damage. Each exacerbation adds airway damage: the infection-inflammation cycle is progressive.

questions.stem: A 44 year old man has had a cough productive of purulent sputum every morning for 8 years, with occasional streaks of blood. He has smoked 5 cigarettes a day for 10 years. His temperature is 36.8°C, pulse rate 76 bpm and oxygen saturation 96% breathing air. He has finger clubbing and coarse crackles at both bases that change after coughing. Chest X-ray shows ring shadows at both bases.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Chronic purulent sputum, haemoptysis, clubbing and coarse crackles with basal ring shadows is bronchiectasis; COPD does not cause clubbing.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

clues: purulent sputum every morning for 8 years
steps.x: Long history of purulent sputum, haemoptysis, clubbing, coarse crackles and ring shadows.

elim: Gives variable wheeze, not daily purulent sputum, haemoptysis and clubbing.
A 5 pack year history is too little, and COPD does not cause clubbing.
Causes clubbing but with a dry cough and fine velcro crackles.
Haemoptysis and clubbing, but 8 years of daily purulent sputum and ring shadows fit dilated airways.

steps.x: B: Bronchiectasis. Clubbing is not a feature of COPD: think bronchiectasis, fibrosis or cancer.

questions.stem: A 39 year old woman has had a cough productive of a cupful of purulent sputum a day for 3 years and two chest infections this winter. She had severe pneumonia at age 6. Her temperature is 36.7°C, pulse rate 74 bpm and oxygen saturation 97% breathing air. Coarse crackles are heard at the left base. Her chest X-ray is reported as normal.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate diagnostic investigation?
questions.e: HRCT confirms bronchiectasis and shows its extent; a normal chest X-ray does not exclude it.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most appropriate diagnostic investigation?

clues: cupful of purulent sputum a day
chest X-ray is reported as normal
steps.x: Suspected bronchiectasis with a normal X-ray.

elim: Used for biopsy or foreign body; it does not show bronchial dilation along the airway.
Looks for pulmonary embolism, not bronchial dilation.
X-ray is insensitive and often normal in bronchiectasis.
Shows obstruction and severity but cannot confirm bronchiectasis.

steps.x: C: High-resolution CT chest. HRCT is the gold-standard test for bronchiectasis.

questions.stem: A 53 year old man has a long history of daily purulent sputum. HRCT is performed. In cross-section, an airway in the right lower lobe is seen as a dilated ring with a small round vessel next to it, so the airway is about twice the diameter of the vessel.
questions.q: Which is the name of this HRCT sign?
questions.e: A dilated bronchus beside a smaller pulmonary artery looks like a signet ring; honeycombing is fibrosis.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the name of this HRCT sign?

clues: dilated ring with a small round vessel next to it
twice the diameter of the vessel
steps.x: Airway (ring) larger than its paired artery (stone) in cross-section.

elim: Ground glass with thickened septa, as in alveolar proteinosis.
Ground glass around a nodule, classically invasive aspergillosis.
Clustered subpleural cysts of end-stage fibrosis such as IPF.
Small branching nodules of small-airway infection, not a dilated bronchus beside its artery.

steps.x: D: Signet ring sign. Signet ring sign: bronchus wider than the adjacent artery, the HRCT hallmark of bronchiectasis.

questions.stem: A 41 year old woman is investigated for a chronic productive cough. HRCT is performed. Running along the length of the lower lobe airways are parallel thick lines that do not taper towards the periphery. In another area, a row of dilated, beaded bronchi is seen.
questions.q: Which condition do these HRCT findings confirm?
questions.e: Tram-track (non-tapering parallel walls) and string of pearls (beaded dilation) are HRCT signs of bronchiectasis.

steps.x: The question asks: Which condition do these HRCT findings confirm?

clues: parallel thick lines that do not taper towards the periphery
steps.x: Tram-tracks and a string of pearls.

elim: Gives basal fibrosis and pleural plaques, not non-tapering airways.
Airway calibre is normal; it is a clinical diagnosis.
Shows basal subpleural honeycombing and reticulation.
Shows hilar nodes and perilymphatic nodules.

steps.x: B: Bronchiectasis. HRCT signs of bronchiectasis: signet ring, tram-track, string of pearls/cluster of grapes.

questions.stem: A 59 year old man with bronchiectasis takes long-term azithromycin but still has frequent exacerbations. His last two courses of antibiotic did not improve his sputum. His temperature is 37.3°C, pulse rate 86 bpm and oxygen saturation 95% breathing air. He is producing purulent sputum.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate investigation to guide his next antibiotic?
questions.e: Sputum culture identifies colonising organisms such as Pseudomonas and their sensitivities, which guides therapy; CRP cannot.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most appropriate investigation to guide his next antibiotic?
Antibiotics are failing: you need the organism and its sensitivities.

elim: Rarely positive in a non-septic exacerbation and do not reflect airway colonisers.
Shows inflammation but not which organism or which antibiotic.
Shows consolidation but cannot identify the organism or its sensitivities.
Suggests bacterial infection but does not guide antibiotic choice.

steps.x: E: Sputum culture and sensitivity. Sputum culture identifies the organism and guides antibiotic choice.

questions.stem: A 19 year old man has newly diagnosed bronchiectasis on HRCT. He has had a productive cough for years, nasal polyps, and loose, oily stools. He is on the 3rd centile for weight. His temperature is 36.8°C and oxygen saturation 95% breathing air. He has finger clubbing.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate investigation to find the cause?
questions.e: Bronchiectasis with steatorrhoea, nasal polyps and poor growth suggests cystic fibrosis; a sweat chloride test (with CFTR genetics) confirms it.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most appropriate investigation to find the cause?
Young, bronchiectasis, malabsorption and polyps = suspected CF.

elim: Screens for primary ciliary dyskinesia, which does not cause steatorrhoea.
No joint disease is described.
Tests for ABPA, which needs asthma.
Worth checking, but steatorrhoea and nasal polyps make CF the target.

steps.x: E: Sweat chloride test. Do CF testing (sweat test) when CF is suspected in bronchiectasis.

questions.stem: A 57 year old woman with bronchiectasis is reviewed in clinic. She is stable between exacerbations but gets breathless climbing stairs and has occasional wheeze. Her respiratory nurse wants to measure how severe her airflow limitation is and to monitor it over time.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate investigation?
questions.e: Spirometry measures and monitors the obstructive defect of bronchiectasis; sputum culture identifies organisms.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most appropriate investigation?

clues: how severe her airflow limitation is
steps.x: Measuring and tracking airflow obstruction.

elim: Shows gas exchange in respiratory failure, not airflow limitation over time.
Insensitive and does not measure airflow.
Assesses the heart, not airflow.
Identifies organisms, not severity of obstruction.

steps.x: D: Spirometry. Spirometry assesses severity in bronchiectasis and shows an obstructive pattern.

questions.stem: A 32 year old woman has just been found to have bronchiectasis on HRCT. She has had pneumonia three times in four years and recurrent ear infections. She has never had asthma and has normal bowels. She is not trying to conceive. Sweat chloride is normal.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate next investigation for the cause?
questions.e: Recurrent sinopulmonary infections with bronchiectasis and a normal sweat test call for serum immunoglobulins to look for immunodeficiency.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most appropriate next investigation for the cause?

clues: pneumonia three times in four years
steps.x: Recurrent bacterial infections: is there antibody deficiency?

elim: Has no role in finding the cause of bronchiectasis.
Looks for pulmonary emboli.
Bronchiectasis is already confirmed; you now need the cause.
A marker of sarcoidosis, not a cause of bronchiectasis.

steps.x: E: Serum immunoglobulins. Check immunoglobulins in every new bronchiectasis: immunodeficiency is treatable.

questions.stem: A 51 year old man has just been diagnosed with bronchiectasis. He coughs up about half a cup of purulent sputum each morning but is not currently having an exacerbation. His temperature is 36.6°C, pulse rate 72 bpm and oxygen saturation 97% breathing air. He asks what he can do every day to help.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate first-line management?
o: Airway clearance with postural drainage taught by a physiotherapist
questions.e: Airway clearance physiotherapy is first-line in bronchiectasis; macrolide prophylaxis is only for frequent exacerbations.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most appropriate first-line management?

clues: what he can do every day
steps.x: Stable, newly diagnosed bronchiectasis with daily sputum.

elim: Steroids are for ABPA, not routine bronchiectasis.
Reserved for 3 or more exacerbations a year despite optimal care.
He is not hypoxic.
Only if disease is confined to one lobe and other measures fail.

steps.x: A: Airway clearance with postural drainage taught by a physiotherapist. Chest physiotherapy (postural drainage and airway clearance) is first-line.

questions.stem: A 60 year old woman with bronchiectasis has done twice-daily airway clearance with an oscillating device for a year, taught by a physiotherapist. She still finds her sputum very thick and hard to clear. She has had one exacerbation in the last year. Her oxygen saturation is 96% breathing air.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate next step to help her clear her sputum?
questions.e: Hypertonic saline draws water into the airway to thin mucus and is an adjunct to physiotherapy; prophylactic antibiotics need 3 or more exacerbations a year.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most appropriate next step to help her clear her sputum?

clues: very thick and hard to clear
one exacerbation in the last year
steps.x: Physiotherapy in place, sputum still thick: add a mucoactive agent.

elim: A cough suppressant would worsen sputum retention.
A bronchodilator; does not thin sputum.
Prophylaxis is not used for one exacerbation a year.
Steroids are for ABPA and do not loosen sputum.

steps.x: B: Inhaled hypertonic saline. Inhaled hypertonic saline is an adjunct to airway clearance.

questions.stem: A 49 year old man with bronchiectasis has 4 days of more purulent sputum and increased cough. His sputum has previously grown Pseudomonas aeruginosa. He is well enough to stay at home. His temperature is 37.5°C, pulse rate 88 bpm, respiratory rate 18 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 95% breathing air. Oral ciprofloxacin is started.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate duration of treatment?
questions.e: Bronchiectasis exacerbations are treated for 14 days; ciprofloxacin covers Pseudomonas. Five days is the course for simple CAP.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most appropriate duration of treatment?

clues: well enough to stay at home
steps.x: Community exacerbation of bronchiectasis.

elim: This is the course for simple community-acquired pneumonia, not bronchiectasis.
Shorter than the standard bronchiectasis course.
Too short for a bronchiectasis exacerbation.
Longer than needed for a community exacerbation.

steps.x: B: Fourteen days. Community exacerbation: 14 days of oral ciprofloxacin.

questions.stem: A 70 year old woman with bronchiectasis has 2 days of feeling very unwell with rigors and copious purulent sputum. Her temperature is 39.4°C, pulse rate 118 bpm, BP 104/66 mmHg, respiratory rate 28 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 91% breathing air. Her sputum has grown Pseudomonas aeruginosa in the past.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate initial management?
o: Oral ciprofloxacin for 14 days at home
Sputum culture and await the result
questions.e: A high fever with tachypnoea makes this a severe exacerbation needing IV antipseudomonal antibiotics; oral ciprofloxacin is for community exacerbations.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most appropriate initial management?
Severe exacerbation: high fever and raised RR.

elim: Does not cover Pseudomonas and she is too unwell for oral treatment.
Right drug class for a mild community exacerbation, but she has high fever and a raised RR.
Steroids are for ABPA, not infective exacerbations.
Send sputum, but treatment must not wait.

steps.x: A: Admit for intravenous antibiotics. IV antibiotics if high fever and raised respiratory rate.

questions.stem: A 38 year old man with asthma has bronchiectasis of the central airways on HRCT. He coughs up brown mucus plugs and his wheeze has worsened. Investigations show eosinophils 1.8 × 10⁹/L, total IgE 2400 kU/L and positive Aspergillus-specific IgE. His temperature is 36.9°C and oxygen saturation 95% breathing air.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate initial management?
questions.e: ABPA is a hypersensitivity reaction to Aspergillus and is treated with oral corticosteroids (itraconazole may be added); antibiotics do not treat it.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most appropriate initial management?
Asthma, eosinophilia, high IgE and Aspergillus IgE = ABPA.

elim: Helps sputum clearance but does not treat the allergic process.
For invasive aspergillosis, not allergic disease.
For frequent bacterial exacerbations.
For a bacterial exacerbation; this is an allergic response to Aspergillus.

steps.x: E: Oral prednisolone. ABPA is treated with corticosteroids.

questions.stem: A 36 year old woman has severe bronchiectasis after an inhaled foreign body as a child. Despite physiotherapy, hypertonic saline and prophylactic azithromycin she has five exacerbations a year and two episodes of haemoptysis. She is fit and well otherwise. Her FEV1 is 85% predicted.
questions.q: Which HRCT finding would most support referral for surgical resection?
o: Central bronchiectasis in both upper lobes
Disease confined to a single lobe
Ground-glass change in both lower lobes
questions.e: Resection is an option when HRCT shows bronchiectasis localised to one lobe in a fit patient with refractory symptoms; diffuse disease is not resectable.

steps.x: The question asks: Which HRCT finding would most support referral for surgical resection?

clues: inhaled foreign body as a child
steps.x: Refractory disease in a fit patient: is it localised?

elim: Widespread disease cannot be removed surgically.
Bilateral disease is not resectable; central disease suggests ABPA.
Not a feature that makes bronchiectasis resectable.
Points to fibrosis, not resectable bronchiectasis.

steps.x: C: Disease confined to a single lobe. Surgery is considered if HRCT shows disease localised to one lobe.

questions.stem: A 64 year old man with bronchiectasis asks about long-term antibiotics to stop his chest infections. He does daily airway clearance and uses hypertonic saline. His sputum has grown Haemophilus influenzae. His respiratory physician explains that prophylaxis is only offered above a set number of exacerbations each year despite optimal management.
questions.q: Which is the minimum number of exacerbations per year at which prophylaxis should be considered?
questions.e: Long-term macrolide (or inhaled antibiotic for Pseudomonas) prophylaxis is considered with 3 or more exacerbations a year despite optimal management.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the minimum number of exacerbations per year at which prophylaxis should be considered?

clues: only offered above a set number of exacerbations
steps.x: Prophylaxis threshold despite optimal care.

elim: Too low; a single exacerbation does not justify long-term antibiotics.
Below the threshold.
Higher than the threshold; prophylaxis is considered earlier.
Far above the threshold.

steps.x: C: 3. Prophylactic antibiotics if 3 or more exacerbations a year despite optimal management.

questions.stem: A 55 year old woman with bronchiectasis is chronically colonised with Pseudomonas aeruginosa. She has had four exacerbations in the last year despite airway clearance physiotherapy and hypertonic saline. A trial of azithromycin had to be stopped because of a prolonged QT interval.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate long-term management to reduce her exacerbations?
questions.e: With 3 or more exacerbations a year and Pseudomonas, an inhaled aminoglycoside (e.g. gentamicin or tobramycin) is used; clarithromycin carries the same QT risk.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most appropriate long-term management to reduce her exacerbations?

clues: four exacerbations in the last year
steps.x: 3 or more exacerbations, Pseudomonas colonised, macrolide not tolerated.

elim: Does not cover Pseudomonas and is not prophylaxis.
A bronchodilator; it does not reduce infective exacerbations.
Another macrolide that also prolongs the QT interval.
Steroids do not prevent bacterial exacerbations and add harm.

steps.x: B: Inhaled gentamicin. Prophylaxis: oral macrolide, or inhaled aminoglycoside for Pseudomonas.

questions.stem: A 72 year old man with bronchiectasis is reviewed by his GP in September. He is stable, does daily airway clearance and has had one exacerbation this year. He has wheeze that improves with salbutamol. He has never been vaccinated against pneumococcus.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate additional preventive measure?
questions.e: Vaccination (annual influenza and pneumococcal) is part of supportive bronchiectasis care; prophylactic antibiotics need 3 or more exacerbations a year.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most appropriate additional preventive measure?
Stable patient due for preventive care.

elim: No role in routine bronchiectasis.
Only after 3 or more exacerbations a year.
He is not described as hypoxic.
Not indicated for stable disease with one exacerbation.

steps.x: B: Influenza and pneumococcal vaccination. Supportive care in bronchiectasis: bronchodilators and vaccination.

questions.stem: A 46 year old woman with bronchiectasis phones her GP surgery. In the last hour she has coughed up about a cupful of fresh bright red blood and is still coughing blood. She feels light-headed. Her pulse rate is 120 bpm and BP 96/60 mmHg.
questions.q: Which is the next most appropriate step in management?
o: Book a routine respiratory clinic appointment
Prescribe oral ciprofloxacin and review in 48 hours
Prescribe oral tranexamic acid at home
questions.e: Massive haemoptysis in bronchiectasis is a medical emergency needing immediate hospital care (ABC, lie on the bleeding side, bronchial artery embolisation).

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the next most appropriate step in management?

clues: a cupful of fresh bright red blood
steps.x: Large-volume haemoptysis with shock.

elim: Delay is dangerous; massive haemoptysis is an emergency.
Far too slow for life-threatening bleeding.
Infection may have triggered it, but bleeding must be managed now.
Home treatment is unsafe with ongoing heavy bleeding and shock.

steps.x: C: Emergency ambulance to hospital. Massive haemoptysis is a medical emergency.

questions.stem: A 61 year old woman with bronchiectasis has daily wheeze and breathlessness walking uphill despite good airway clearance. She has had two exacerbations this year. Spirometry shows FEV1/FVC 0.62 with a 14% improvement after salbutamol. Her oxygen saturation is 96% breathing air.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate addition to her treatment?
questions.e: Bronchodilators help wheeze and breathlessness in bronchiectasis; with only two exacerbations a year she does not meet the threshold for prophylaxis.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most appropriate addition to her treatment?
Wheeze with reversible airflow obstruction; exacerbations below threshold.

elim: Prophylaxis is reserved for 3 or more exacerbations a year.
Prophylaxis is reserved for 3 or more exacerbations a year.
She is not hypoxic.
No ABPA is described; long-term steroids are not used.

steps.x: A: Inhaled bronchodilator. Bronchodilators are supportive treatment for breathlessness and wheeze in bronchiectasis.

questions.stem: A 45 year old man developed bronchiectasis after a severe necrotising pneumonia in his twenties. He asks why his airways keep getting worse when the original infection was cured long ago. His consultant explains the self-perpetuating process in his airways.
questions.q: Which is the most likely mechanism of progression?
o: Cycle of infection, inflammation and impaired mucociliary clearance
Fibroblast proliferation in the alveolar interstitium
Smooth muscle hypertrophy narrowing the airway
questions.e: The vicious cycle of infection, inflammation and impaired mucociliary clearance destroys the elastic and muscular wall, causing irreversible, progressive dilation.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most likely mechanism of progression?
An initial insult starts a self-sustaining loop.

elim: Not the mechanism of post-infective bronchiectasis.
That is interstitial fibrosis.
That is asthma; it does not dilate bronchi.
Bronchiectatic airways are dilated, not narrowed.

steps.x: B: Cycle of infection, inflammation and impaired mucociliary clearance. Infection, inflammation and poor clearance feed each other and destroy the bronchial wall.

questions.stem: A 58 year old woman with bronchiectasis has grown Pseudomonas aeruginosa from her sputum on six occasions over 3 years, despite courses of ciprofloxacin. Each exacerbation grows the same organism. Her HRCT shows widespread dilated airways filled with mucus.
questions.q: Which best explains why the same organism keeps recurring?
o: Haematogenous spread from a distant focus
Mucus pooling in dilated airways allows chronic colonisation
Reinfection from her family each time
Spontaneous mutation of airway commensals into Pseudomonas
questions.e: Dilated airways pool mucus, giving a nidus for chronic colonisation by H. influenzae and Pseudomonas, which perpetuates infection and damage.

steps.x: The question asks: Which best explains why the same organism keeps recurring?

clues: widespread dilated airways filled with mucus
steps.x: Damaged, dilated, mucus-filled airways.

elim: Pseudomonas does not cause systemic antibody deficiency.
Airway colonisers come from the airway itself, not the blood.
The organism persists in her own damaged airways.
Bacteria do not change species.

steps.x: C: Mucus pooling in dilated airways allows chronic colonisation. Pooled mucus in dilated airways is a nidus for chronic colonisation (H. influenzae, Pseudomonas).

questions.stem: A 16 year old girl with cystic fibrosis has bronchiectasis and chronic Pseudomonas infection. Her FEV1 is 68% predicted and she uses airway clearance twice daily. Her genetic testing shows she is homozygous for the F508del variant. She asks why her disease affects her lungs.
questions.q: Which is the most likely mechanism of her airway disease?
o: Absent dynein arms in the cilia
Excess sodium chloride in airway secretions
Loss of IgA secretion into the airway
Reduced chloride secretion producing thick, dehydrated mucus
questions.e: Defective CFTR chloride channels reduce chloride and water secretion, making thick, dehydrated mucus that cannot be cleared and predisposes to chronic infection.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most likely mechanism of her airway disease?
F508del = defective CFTR chloride channel.

elim: That is primary ciliary dyskinesia.
Causes emphysema, not CF.
CFTR failure reduces chloride secretion; sweat, not mucus, is salty.
Not the defect in CF.

steps.x: E: Reduced chloride secretion producing thick, dehydrated mucus. Defective CFTR gives thick, dehydrated mucus that cannot be cleared.

questions.stem: A 52 year old man has had bronchiectasis for 30 years. He needed a right lower lobectomy for recurrent haemoptysis and repeated infections. The resected lobe shows bronchial walls with loss of elastic tissue and cartilage, heavy neutrophil infiltration and dilated lumens full of pus.
questions.q: Which is the most likely cause of the destruction of the bronchial wall?
o: Asbestos fibres in the bronchial wall
Proteases released by neutrophils digesting elastin and cartilage
questions.e: Neutrophil proteases (e.g. elastase) and mediators digest elastin and cartilage in the bronchial wall, causing irreversible dilation.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most likely cause of the destruction of the bronchial wall?

clues: loss of elastic tissue and cartilage
steps.x: Neutrophils plus loss of elastin and cartilage.

elim: Asbestos causes fibrosis and pleural disease.
That is fibrosis, which stiffens rather than dilates the airway.
Seen in sarcoidosis or TB, not the neutrophil picture described.
Not the mechanism of bronchiectasis.

steps.x: E: Proteases released by neutrophils digesting elastin and cartilage. Chronic inflammation releases proteases that digest elastin and cartilage, so the wall dilates irreversibly.

questions.stem: A 24 year old man has bronchiectasis, chronic sinusitis and infertility. He has had a wet cough every day since early childhood. Semen analysis shows normal sperm numbers but the sperm are immotile. Electron microscopy of a nasal brushing shows abnormal cilia.
questions.q: Which is the most likely mechanism of his bronchiectasis?
o: Impaired mucociliary clearance from defective ciliary beating
questions.e: In primary ciliary dyskinesia, defective ciliary beating impairs mucociliary clearance, starting the cycle of infection and inflammation that dilates the bronchi.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most likely mechanism of his bronchiectasis?
Immotile sperm + abnormal cilia = primary ciliary dyskinesia.

elim: His defect is in the cilia, not immunoglobulins.
CF causes obstructive azoospermia (absent vas), not immotile sperm with abnormal cilia.
That is ABPA in asthmatics.
Alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency causes emphysema.

steps.x: D: Impaired mucociliary clearance from defective ciliary beating. Poor mucociliary clearance starts the infection-inflammation cycle.
